aws_elasti_cache_subnet_group: `aws_elasti_cache_subnet_group` defines the real VPC subnets an `aws_elasti_cache_cache_cluster` or `aws_elasti_cache_replication_group`'s nodes are actually placed into, required network placement before either can be created.
aws_elasti_cache_user: `aws_elasti_cache_user` defines a real Redis ACL-based user identity, with its own authentication and permitted commands and key patterns, for an `aws_elasti_cache_replication_group` running Redis's own role-based access control rather than one shared password for every client.
aws_elasti_cache_user_group: `aws_elasti_cache_user_group` collects `aws_elasti_cache_user`s into a real, named group that gets applied to an `aws_elasti_cache_replication_group` together, rather than a caller attaching each user to the replication group individually.
aws_elastic_beanstalk_application: `aws_elastic_beanstalk_application` is the real, top-level Elastic Beanstalk container an `aws_elastic_beanstalk_application_version` and `aws_elastic_beanstalk_environment` both belong to, the logical grouping for every deployed version of one caller application.
aws_elastic_beanstalk_application_versio: `aws_elastic_beanstalk_application_version` is one real, specific, immutable build of an `aws_elastic_beanstalk_application`'s own code, stored in S3, that an `aws_elastic_beanstalk_environment` actually deploys.
aws_elastic_beanstalk_configuration_temp: `aws_elastic_beanstalk_configuration_template` is a real, reusable set of environment configuration options for an `aws_elastic_beanstalk_application`, instance type, scaling settings, environment variables, that an `aws_elastic_beanstalk_environment` can be created from rather than every environment being configured from scratch.
aws_elastic_beanstalk_environment: `aws_elastic_beanstalk_environment` is the real, actual running deployment, provisioning and managing the underlying EC2 instances, load balancer, and Auto Scaling group on a caller's behalf, that an `aws_elastic_beanstalk_application_version` gets deployed into.
aws_elastic_load_balancing_load_balancer: `aws_elastic_load_balancing_load_balancer` creates a Classic Load Balancer, ELB's original, legacy load balancing resource, layer 4 and basic layer 7 routing, superseded for new deployments by `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_load_balancer`'s own Application and Network Load Balancer types.
aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener: `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener` checks for real connection requests on a specific port and protocol against an `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_load_balancer`, the actual entry point that `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener_rule`s route matching traffic from.
aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener_c: `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener_certificate` attaches an additional real TLS certificate to an `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener` beyond its own default certificate, needed when a listener must serve multiple domain names with SNI.
aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener_r: `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener_rule` routes a real, matching request, by path, host header, or other condition, on an `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener` to a specific `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_target_group`, letting one listener serve several different backend services.
aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_load_balan: `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_load_balancer` creates a real Application Load Balancer or Network Load Balancer, ELB's current generation, that an `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener` actually receives and routes traffic through.
aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_target_gro: `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_target_group` is the real, actual set of EC2 instances, IP addresses, or Lambda functions an `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener_rule` routes matching traffic to, with its own health checks determining which targets are currently eligible to receive it.
aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_trust_stor: `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_trust_store` is a real repository of CA certificates an `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_listener` validates client certificates against for mutual TLS, the ALB-side equivalent of a CloudFront trust store.

`aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_trust_store_revocation` loads a real certificate revocation list into an `aws_elastic_load_balancing_v2_trust_store`, so a client certificate that's been revoked is rejected during mutual TLS even if it still chains to a trusted CA.
aws_elasticsearch_domain: `aws_elasticsearch_domain` provisions a search and analytics domain using the legacy `AWS::Elasticsearch::Domain` CloudFormation resource type. Amazon Elasticsearch Service was renamed Amazon OpenSearch Service on September 8, 2021; this legacy resource type still functions and supports open-source Elasticsearch, but AWS recommends the newer `AWS::OpenSearchService::Domain` resource, which supports both OpenSearch and Elasticsearch, for new domains.
aws_elemental_inference_feed: `aws_elemental_inference_feed` is the top-level real resource in AWS Elemental Inference, a fully managed AI service that transforms live broadcast video in parallel with encoding into vertical crops and highlight clips for mobile and social platforms, TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts among them, in real time. A feed starts in a CREATING state and becomes AVAILABLE once ready to configure outputs against. AWS Elemental Inference reached general availability February 24, 2026, genuinely new enough that this session verified it live rather than trusting a remembered description.
aws_emr_cluster: `aws_emr_cluster` provisions a real, managed Hadoop/Spark cluster, EC2 instances running the actual big-data processing frameworks, that an `aws_emr_step` or an EMR Studio notebook runs work against.
aws_emr_instance_fleet_config: `aws_emr_instance_fleet_config` defines a real, flexible mix of instance types and purchasing options, On-Demand and Spot together, for one role inside an `aws_emr_cluster`, EMR's newer, more flexible alternative to `aws_emr_instance_group_config`'s single-instance-type model.
aws_emr_instance_group_config: `aws_emr_instance_group_config` defines one real group of uniformly configured EC2 instances, master, core, or task, inside an `aws_emr_cluster`, EMR's original instance-provisioning model.
aws_emr_step: `aws_emr_step` submits one real unit of processing work, a Spark job, a Hive query, to a running `aws_emr_cluster`, executed in the order steps are added.
aws_emr_studio: `aws_emr_studio` provisions a real, web-based integrated development environment for data scientists and analysts to develop, visualize, and debug data engineering and analytics applications, connecting to `aws_emr_cluster`s and EMR on EKS virtual clusters as compute backends.
aws_emr_studio_session_mapping: `aws_emr_studio_session_mapping` maps a real IAM Identity Center user or group to an `aws_emr_studio`, with an attached session policy refining exactly what that user or group can do inside the Studio.
aws_emr_walworkspace: `aws_emr_walworkspace` is a real, durable, managed storage layer, outliving any single `aws_emr_cluster`, that Apache HBase write-ahead logs get written into, so a caller can point a brand-new cluster at the same S3 root directory and WAL workspace after a cluster or Availability Zone failure and recover unflushed HBase data within minutes.
aws_emrcontainers_endpoint: `aws_emrcontainers_endpoint` is a real, managed gateway connecting an `aws_emr_studio` to an `aws_emrcontainers_virtual_cluster`, so Studio's notebooks can actually communicate with and submit interactive work to that virtual cluster.
aws_emrcontainers_security_configuration: `aws_emrcontainers_security_configuration` is a real, reusable security setup, including AWS Lake Formation integration, that gets applied to an `aws_emrcontainers_virtual_cluster` when it's created, rather than every virtual cluster's security being configured individually.
aws_emrcontainers_virtual_cluster: `aws_emrcontainers_virtual_cluster` registers a real Amazon EKS namespace as an EMR on EKS virtual cluster, the actual target Spark and Hive jobs submitted through EMR on EKS run against, using the underlying Kubernetes cluster's own compute rather than dedicated EMR instances.
aws_emrserverless_application: `aws_emrserverless_application` runs real Spark or Hive jobs with automatically provisioned and scaled compute, no `aws_emr_cluster` to size, launch, or terminate, EMR's serverless alternative for workloads that don't need persistent cluster infrastructure.
aws_entity_resolution_id_mapping_workflo: `aws_entity_resolution_id_mapping_workflow` links real entity IDs across two different `aws_entity_resolution_id_namespace`s, AWS Entity Resolution's dedicated workflow for cross-namespace identity mapping, distinct from `aws_entity_resolution_matching_workflow`'s own general record-matching purpose.
aws_entity_resolution_id_namespace: `aws_entity_resolution_id_namespace` defines a real, distinct source of entity identifiers, one party's own customer ID space, for instance, that an `aws_entity_resolution_id_mapping_workflow` maps against another namespace's own identifiers.
aws_entity_resolution_matching_workflow: `aws_entity_resolution_matching_workflow` is the real, actual sequence AWS Entity Resolution runs to match records from an `aws_entity_resolution_schema_mapping`-defined input, using rule-based, machine-learning, or data-service-provider matching, and write consolidated, linked output to S3.
aws_entity_resolution_policy_statement: `aws_entity_resolution_policy_statement` is a real, resource-based access policy statement controlling which other AWS principals can use an `aws_entity_resolution_matching_workflow` or `aws_entity_resolution_schema_mapping`, needed for cross-account Entity Resolution use, including from within an AWS Clean Rooms collaboration.
aws_entity_resolution_schema_mapping: `aws_entity_resolution_schema_mapping` defines which real input fields from an AWS Glue table an `aws_entity_resolution_matching_workflow` actually uses for matching, either a caller's own custom schema or one brought directly from an existing Glue input.
aws_event_schemas_discoverer: `aws_event_schemas_discoverer` automatically infers real event schemas from an `aws_events_event_bus`'s own live traffic and adds them to a registry, so a caller doesn't have to write every event schema by hand from a sample payload.
aws_event_schemas_registry: `aws_event_schemas_registry` is a real, named collection of event schemas, the container every `aws_event_schemas_schema` in one logical group of related events belongs to, separate from the default registry EventBridge maintains automatically.
aws_event_schemas_registry_policy: `aws_event_schemas_registry_policy` is a real, resource-based access policy controlling which other AWS accounts can view or use the schemas in an `aws_event_schemas_registry`, needed for sharing a schema registry across accounts.
aws_event_schemas_schema: `aws_event_schemas_schema` is one real, versioned schema definition, OpenAPI or JSONSchema, inside an `aws_event_schemas_registry`, describing the actual structure of one type of event so code bindings can be generated against it.
aws_events_api_destination: `aws_events_api_destination` is a real HTTP endpoint target an `aws_events_rule` can invoke directly, the mechanism for routing matched events to a third-party API without a Lambda function in between just to make the HTTP call.
aws_events_archive: `aws_events_archive` continuously and automatically saves real events flowing through an `aws_events_event_bus`, matching an optional filter, so they can be replayed back onto the bus later, real event replay rather than events being lost the moment they're processed once.
aws_events_connection: `aws_events_connection` stores the real authorization credentials, API key, OAuth, basic auth, that an `aws_events_api_destination` uses to actually authenticate its calls, kept separate so the same credentials can be reused across multiple destinations.
aws_events_endpoint: `aws_events_endpoint` is a real, global EventBridge endpoint backed by event buses in two Regions, that automatically fails over which Region actually receives events, real multi-Region resiliency for event-driven applications that can't tolerate one Region's event bus being unavailable.
aws_events_event_bus: `aws_events_event_bus` is the real, actual router events flow through, custom, partner, or the default account event bus, that every `aws_events_rule` is defined against and matches incoming events on.
aws_events_rule: `aws_events_rule` matches real events flowing through an `aws_events_event_bus` against a defined pattern, or fires on a schedule, and routes matching events to one or more real targets, a Lambda function, an SQS queue, a Step Functions state machine.
aws_evidently_experiment: `aws_evidently_experiment` ran a real A/B test, splitting traffic across an `aws_evidently_feature`'s variations and measuring the effect on defined metrics, inside an `aws_evidently_project`. Discontinued along with the rest of CloudWatch Evidently on October 17, 2025.
aws_evidently_feature: `aws_evidently_feature` defined a real feature flag with its own variations inside an `aws_evidently_project`. Like every other Evidently resource, it stopped being accessible when AWS discontinued the service on October 17, 2025.
aws_evidently_launch: `aws_evidently_launch` gradually rolled out an `aws_evidently_feature`'s variations to an increasing percentage of real traffic inside an `aws_evidently_project`. Discontinued along with the rest of CloudWatch Evidently on October 17, 2025.
aws_evidently_project: `aws_evidently_project` was the top-level CloudWatch Evidently resource that an `aws_evidently_feature`, `aws_evidently_experiment`, `aws_evidently_launch`, and `aws_evidently_segment` all belonged to. AWS discontinued CloudWatch Evidently on October 17, 2025; the console and Evidently resources are no longer accessible, and AWS directs customers who need feature-flag and A/B-experiment capability to AWS AppConfig instead.
aws_evidently_segment: `aws_evidently_segment` defined a real, named subset of users, by attribute, that an `aws_evidently_experiment` or `aws_evidently_launch` could target inside an `aws_evidently_project`. Discontinued along with the rest of CloudWatch Evidently on October 17, 2025.
aws_evs_environment: `aws_evs_environment` deploys a real VMware Cloud Foundation stack, SDDC Manager, NSX Manager, vCenter Server, and an initial set of ESXi hosts, directly on EC2 bare-metal instances inside a caller's own VPC, letting existing VMware-based workloads migrate to AWS unmodified rather than needing conversion to a different hypervisor.
aws_fin_space_environment: `aws_fin_space_environment` provisions a real Amazon FinSpace environment, a managed data catalog and analytics workspace, notebook-based, kdb Insights, or dataset-browser, purpose-built for financial industry data. Amazon FinSpace closed to new customers on October 7, 2025, with end of support scheduled for October 7, 2026; existing customers can continue using it in the interim.
aws_fis_experiment_template: `aws_fis_experiment_template` defines a real chaos engineering experiment for AWS Fault Injection Service, which actions to inject, terminating instances, throttling an API, spiking CPU, against which real targets, and what stop conditions abort the experiment automatically if things go wrong.
aws_flow_log: `aws_flow_log` captures real IP traffic metadata, source, destination, port, protocol, accept or reject, flowing through a VPC, subnet, or individual network interface, delivered to S3 or CloudWatch Logs, real, ongoing network visibility for troubleshooting and security analysis without capturing packet contents themselves.
aws_fms_policy: `aws_fms_policy` defines a real, centrally managed security policy, WAF rules, security group settings, Shield Advanced protection, that AWS Firewall Manager automatically applies and keeps enforced across every account and resource in an AWS Organization matching the policy's scope.
aws_fms_resource_set: `aws_fms_resource_set` is a real, named collection of specific resources that an `aws_fms_policy` can reference directly, scoping a policy to an explicit resource list rather than only a broader tag- or account-based filter.
aws_forecast_dataset: `aws_forecast_dataset` held real historical time-series data inside an `aws_forecast_dataset_group` that Amazon Forecast trained a predictor against. Like the rest of Forecast, closed to new customers since July 29, 2024.
aws_forecast_dataset_group: `aws_forecast_dataset_group` was the top-level container an `aws_forecast_dataset` belonged to in Amazon Forecast, AWS's managed time-series forecasting service. Amazon Forecast closed to new customers on July 29, 2024; existing customers can continue using it, with AWS recommending Amazon SageMaker Canvas for new time-series forecasting work.
aws_fraud_detector_detector: `aws_fraud_detector_detector` was the real, top-level Amazon Fraud Detector resource combining an `aws_fraud_detector_event_type`, a trained model, and business rules to actually score real-time fraud risk. Amazon Fraud Detector closed to new customers on November 7, 2025; existing customers can continue using it, with AWS pointing to Amazon SageMaker, AutoGluon, or AWS WAF Fraud Control for new fraud-detection work.
aws_fraud_detector_entity_type: `aws_fraud_detector_entity_type` categorized who or what performed a real event, a customer, a merchant, that an `aws_fraud_detector_event_type` referenced. Closed to new customers along with the rest of Fraud Detector since November 7, 2025.
aws_fraud_detector_event_type: `aws_fraud_detector_event_type` defined the real structure, entity type, variables, labels, of one category of event, a login, a transaction, that an `aws_fraud_detector_detector` was configured to actually evaluate. Like the rest of Fraud Detector, closed to new customers since November 7, 2025.
aws_fraud_detector_label: `aws_fraud_detector_label` tagged real historical events as fraudulent or legitimate for training an `aws_fraud_detector_event_type`'s own model. Closed to new customers along with the rest of Fraud Detector since November 7, 2025.
aws_fraud_detector_outcome: `aws_fraud_detector_outcome` defined a real possible result, approve, review, block, that an `aws_fraud_detector_detector`'s own business rules could return for an evaluated event. Closed to new customers along with the rest of Fraud Detector since November 7, 2025.
aws_fraud_detector_variable: `aws_fraud_detector_variable` defined one real input field, an IP address, an email domain, a transaction amount, used by an `aws_fraud_detector_event_type`'s model and rules. Closed to new customers along with the rest of Fraud Detector since November 7, 2025.
aws_fsx_data_repository_association: `aws_fsx_data_repository_association` links an `aws_fsx_file_system` (FSx for Lustre) to a real S3 bucket, automatically and transparently presenting S3 objects as files and syncing changes in either direction, so Lustre can be used as a high-performance compute layer directly over data that lives durably in S3.
aws_fsx_file_system: `aws_fsx_file_system` provisions a real, fully managed file system, Windows File Server, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, or OpenZFS, each a genuinely different underlying file system technology rather than variants of one engine, chosen based on the workload's own protocol and performance needs.
aws_fsx_s3_access_point_attachment: `aws_fsx_s3_access_point_attachment` exposes an `aws_fsx_file_system`'s data through a real S3 access point, so applications that already speak the S3 API can read and write FSx-backed data without switching to a file protocol like NFS or SMB.
aws_fsx_snapshot: `aws_fsx_snapshot` is a real, point-in-time, incremental backup of an `aws_fsx_file_system` (FSx for OpenZFS), restorable to a new volume or file system without copying unchanged data every time.
aws_fsx_storage_virtual_machine: `aws_fsx_storage_virtual_machine` is a real, independent virtual file server, with its own security style and network endpoint, running inside an `aws_fsx_file_system` (FSx for ONTAP), the NetApp SVM concept AWS FSx exposes directly.
aws_fsx_volume: `aws_fsx_volume` is a real, logical storage container, with its own size and data-management policies, created inside an `aws_fsx_file_system` (ONTAP or OpenZFS), the actual unit shares and mount points are exported from rather than the whole file system.
aws_game_lift_alias: `aws_game_lift_alias` points a stable, real identifier at a specific `aws_game_lift_fleet`, letting a caller redirect matchmaking and game clients to a new fleet, a blue/green deployment or a fleet in a different Region, without changing anything on the client side.
aws_game_lift_build: `aws_game_lift_build` uploads a real, packaged game server executable and its dependencies to GameLift, the actual software an `aws_game_lift_fleet`'s EC2 instances run to host game sessions.
aws_game_lift_container_fleet: `aws_game_lift_container_fleet` runs real, containerized game server applications, defined by an `aws_game_lift_container_group_definition`, on managed EC2 instances, GameLift's container-native alternative to `aws_game_lift_fleet`'s own executable-based deployment model.
aws_game_lift_container_group_definition: `aws_game_lift_container_group_definition` is the real, versioned blueprint an `aws_game_lift_container_fleet` deploys from, which container images to run per instance and how, game-server containers plus any supporting per-instance containers like logging or background services.
aws_game_lift_fleet: `aws_game_lift_fleet` provisions real EC2 instances running an `aws_game_lift_build`'s game server executable, GameLift's original, EC2-based compute model for hosting multiplayer game sessions at scale.
aws_game_lift_game_server_group: `aws_game_lift_game_server_group` runs GameLift FleetIQ on top of a real, self-managed EC2 Auto Scaling group, optimizing for Spot Instance savings while protecting instances that are still hosting active game sessions from early termination.
aws_game_lift_game_session_queue: `aws_game_lift_game_session_queue` routes a real player's game session placement request to whichever `aws_game_lift_fleet`, across multiple fleets and locations, can host it fastest or cheapest, according to the queue's own defined priority order.
aws_game_lift_location: `aws_game_lift_location` registers a real, custom location, a caller's own data center or an unsupported AWS Region, that an `aws_game_lift_fleet` running in Anywhere mode can actually be deployed to.
aws_game_lift_matchmaking_configuration: `aws_game_lift_matchmaking_configuration` defines a real FlexMatch matchmaking pool, including which `aws_game_lift_matchmaking_rule_set` it evaluates candidate players against and which `aws_game_lift_game_session_queue` a completed match gets placed through.
aws_game_lift_matchmaking_rule_set: `aws_game_lift_matchmaking_rule_set` defines the real, JSON-based rules, team size, skill balancing, latency requirements, that an `aws_game_lift_matchmaking_configuration` actually evaluates candidate players against to form a match.
aws_game_lift_script: `aws_game_lift_script` uploads real server-side logic for GameLift Realtime Servers, a lighter-weight alternative to `aws_game_lift_build`'s full custom executable for game logic that fits GameLift's own managed network layer.
aws_global_accelerator_accelerator: `aws_global_accelerator_accelerator` creates two real, static anycast IP addresses that route traffic over AWS's own global network backbone to the closest healthy endpoint, real, consistent public entry points independent of the endpoints' own Regions or IP addresses changing behind them.
aws_global_accelerator_cross_account_att: `aws_global_accelerator_cross_account_attachment` authorizes a real, specific set of endpoint resources owned by another AWS account to be added to this account's own `aws_global_accelerator_accelerator`, a real cross-account grant rather than every accelerator needing to live in the same account as every endpoint it targets.
aws_global_accelerator_endpoint_group: `aws_global_accelerator_endpoint_group` is the real, specific set of endpoints, ALBs, NLBs, EC2 instances, Elastic IPs, in one AWS Region that an `aws_global_accelerator_listener` routes matching traffic to, with health checks determining which endpoints actually receive it.
aws_global_accelerator_listener: `aws_global_accelerator_listener` checks for real connection requests on a specific port and protocol against an `aws_global_accelerator_accelerator`, the entry point `aws_global_accelerator_endpoint_group`s route matching traffic from.
aws_glue_blueprint: `aws_glue_blueprint` packages a real, reusable workflow template, generating a full set of `aws_glue_job`s, crawlers, and triggers from a small set of caller-provided parameters, rather than a caller assembling the same recurring pipeline shape by hand each time.
aws_glue_catalog: `aws_glue_catalog` is a real, top-level metadata catalog, the container every `aws_glue_database` and `aws_glue_table` in one Glue Data Catalog deployment actually belongs to, queryable directly by Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR without a caller copying the same metadata into each service separately.
aws_glue_classifier: `aws_glue_classifier` tells an `aws_glue_crawler` how to actually recognize and parse a real data format, CSV with a specific delimiter, a custom log format, beyond the built-in classifiers Glue already provides.
aws_glue_connection: `aws_glue_connection` stores the real, actual connection details, JDBC URL, credentials, network placement, an `aws_glue_crawler` or `aws_glue_job` uses to reach a data source outside the Glue Data Catalog itself.
aws_glue_crawler: `aws_glue_crawler` scans a real data source, S3, a JDBC database, DynamoDB, and automatically infers and populates an `aws_glue_table`'s own schema in the Glue Data Catalog, rather than a caller writing that schema by hand.
aws_glue_database: `aws_glue_database` is a real, logical grouping of `aws_glue_table`s inside an `aws_glue_catalog`, organizing related tables the way a schema organizes tables in a traditional relational database.
aws_glue_dev_endpoint: `aws_glue_dev_endpoint` provisions a real, persistent development environment for interactively writing and testing an `aws_glue_job`'s own ETL script before running it as an actual, scheduled job.
aws_glue_integration: `aws_glue_integration` defines a real, zero-ETL integration from a source, Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, to a target like Redshift or OpenSearch, replicating and keeping data in sync without a caller writing or scheduling any ETL job themselves. AWS Glue added CloudFormation and CDK support for zero-ETL integrations in November 2025.
aws_glue_integration_resource_property: `aws_glue_integration_resource_property` sets a real, shared configuration property applied to every `aws_glue_integration` built from the same underlying resource, changing it affects every integration that resource is a part of rather than one integration individually.
aws_glue_job: `aws_glue_job` defines a real, actual ETL script, Spark or Python, that transforms data read from a source into a target, run on demand, on a schedule via `aws_glue_trigger`, or as part of a larger workflow.
aws_glue_mltransform: `aws_glue_mltransform` trains a real, managed machine-learning model, FindMatches, that an `aws_glue_job` can use to deduplicate or link records that don't match exactly, fuzzy matching a rule-based transform can't express.
aws_glue_partition: `aws_glue_partition` registers one real, physical subdivision of an `aws_glue_table`'s data, a specific date or Region's worth of files, for instance, so a query engine can skip reading partitions that don't match a query's filter instead of scanning the entire table.
aws_glue_registry: `aws_glue_registry` is a real, named collection of related `aws_glue_schema`s in the Glue Schema Registry, organizing schemas the way an `aws_glue_catalog` organizes tables.
aws_glue_schema: `aws_glue_schema` is a real, versioned schema definition, Avro, JSON, or Protobuf, registered so producers and consumers of streaming data, Kinesis or MSK, agree on and validate against the same actual message structure.
aws_glue_security_configuration: `aws_glue_security_configuration` sets real encryption settings, at rest and in transit, applied to an `aws_glue_job`, `aws_glue_crawler`, or development endpoint when it runs, kept as its own reusable resource rather than repeated per job.
aws_glue_table: `aws_glue_table` registers the real schema, columns, types, storage format and location, of one dataset in the Glue Data Catalog, metadata a query engine reads to know how to actually read the underlying data in S3 or elsewhere.
aws_glue_table_optimizer: `aws_glue_table_optimizer` automatically runs real, background maintenance, compacting small files, expiring old snapshots, deleting orphaned files, against an Apache Iceberg `aws_glue_table`, storage and query-performance upkeep a caller would otherwise have to schedule and run manually.
aws_glue_trigger: `aws_glue_trigger` starts an `aws_glue_job` or `aws_glue_crawler` on a real, defined schedule, on demand, or when another job or crawler completes, the actual mechanism that turns standalone Glue resources into a chained pipeline.
aws_glue_usage_profile: `aws_glue_usage_profile` sets real, preventative cost-control limits, worker count, session parameters, that apply automatically to every Glue job or interactive session an assigned IAM user or role creates, letting an admin give a test user a tighter cap than a production data engineer without either having to self-police. Reached general availability June 2024.
aws_glue_user_defined_function: `aws_glue_user_defined_function` registers a real, custom function, callable from Athena or Spark SQL, in an `aws_glue_catalog`, extending what a query engine can compute beyond its own built-in functions.
aws_grafana_workspace: `aws_grafana_workspace` provisions a real, managed Grafana server, Amazon Managed Grafana, with its own authentication, data source connections, and dashboards, without a caller running and patching Grafana on their own compute.
aws_greengrass_connector_definition: `aws_greengrass_connector_definition` deploys a real, pre-built AWS integration, connecting to a local ML model or a serial port, for instance, to an `aws_greengrass_group`'s core device without a caller writing that integration logic themselves. Part of Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_connector_definition_vers: `aws_greengrass_connector_definition_version` is a real, specific version of an `aws_greengrass_connector_definition`, part of AWS IoT Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_core_definition: `aws_greengrass_core_definition` registers the real primary device, running the actual AWS IoT Greengrass V1 core software, that hosts an `aws_greengrass_group`'s local compute and connects it to AWS IoT Core. Part of Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023, ahead of its October 2026 end of support.
aws_greengrass_core_definition_version: `aws_greengrass_core_definition_version` is a real, specific version of an `aws_greengrass_core_definition`, part of AWS IoT Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_device_definition: `aws_greengrass_device_definition` registers real, local IoT devices, connected to an `aws_greengrass_group`'s core rather than directly to AWS IoT Core, that can communicate with the core and each other even when internet connectivity is lost. Part of Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_device_definition_version: `aws_greengrass_device_definition_version` is a real, specific version of an `aws_greengrass_device_definition`, part of AWS IoT Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_function_definition: `aws_greengrass_function_definition` lists the real Lambda functions an `aws_greengrass_group`'s core device runs locally, at the edge, rather than in the AWS Cloud. Part of Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_function_definition_versi: `aws_greengrass_function_definition_version` is a real, specific version of an `aws_greengrass_function_definition`, part of AWS IoT Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_group: `aws_greengrass_group` is the real, top-level container in AWS IoT Greengrass V1 that a core device, its Lambda functions, subscriptions, and other local resources all belong to, deployed together as one unit. AWS IoT Greengrass V1 entered its extended-life, maintenance-only phase on June 30, 2023 (no further feature, enhancement, or security updates) and reaches full end of support on October 7, 2026; devices already running V1 continue operating and connecting to the cloud in the meantime, and AWS recommends migrating to AWS IoT Greengrass V2 for new work.
aws_greengrass_group_version: `aws_greengrass_group_version` is a real, specific, versioned snapshot of an `aws_greengrass_group`'s own configuration, the actual deployable unit pushed to a core device, part of AWS IoT Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_logger_definition: `aws_greengrass_logger_definition` configures real, local logging, destination and log level, for an `aws_greengrass_group`'s core device and its Lambda functions. Part of Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_logger_definition_version: `aws_greengrass_logger_definition_version` is a real, specific version of an `aws_greengrass_logger_definition`, part of AWS IoT Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_resource_definition: `aws_greengrass_resource_definition` gives an `aws_greengrass_group`'s Lambda functions real, controlled access to local resources, a machine learning model, a device volume, a secret, that live on the core device itself rather than in the cloud. Part of Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_resource_definition_versi: `aws_greengrass_resource_definition_version` is a real, specific version of an `aws_greengrass_resource_definition`, part of AWS IoT Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_subscription_definition: `aws_greengrass_subscription_definition` defines real, local MQTT-style publish/subscribe routes between an `aws_greengrass_group`'s core, its devices, its Lambda functions, and the cloud, the actual message-routing rules the group runs on. Part of Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_subscription_definition_v: `aws_greengrass_subscription_definition_version` is a real, specific version of an `aws_greengrass_subscription_definition`, part of AWS IoT Greengrass V1's maintenance-only lifecycle since June 2023.
aws_greengrass_v2_component_version: `aws_greengrass_v2_component_version` is a real, versioned software module, AWS-provided or a caller's own, deployed to AWS IoT Greengrass V2 core devices through an `aws_greengrass_v2_deployment`, V2's software-component model that replaced V1's separate function, connector, and resource definitions with one unified concept.
aws_greengrass_v2_deployment: `aws_greengrass_v2_deployment` pushes a real, defined set of `aws_greengrass_v2_component_version`s to a target group of Greengrass V2 core devices, with rollout and rollback configuration, the actual mechanism that gets software running on real edge devices.
aws_ground_station_config: `aws_ground_station_config` defines one real, specific piece of a satellite contact, antenna downlink parameters, tracking, dataflow endpoint details, that an `aws_ground_station_mission_profile` combines several of into a complete contact plan.
aws_ground_station_dataflow_endpoint_gro: `aws_ground_station_dataflow_endpoint_group` registers the real network endpoints, an AWS Ground Station Agent endpoint or traditional dataflow endpoints, that satellite data actually flows to or from during a contact.

`aws_ground_station_dataflow_endpoint_group_v2` is the newer resource type for the same real concept as `aws_ground_station_dataflow_endpoint_group`, restricted specifically to AWS Ground Station Agent-based endpoints rather than the original's broader mix of endpoint types, endpoints within one group must all be the same type either way.
aws_ground_station_mission_profile: `aws_ground_station_mission_profile` combines one or more `aws_ground_station_config`s into a real, reusable, complete contact plan, antenna, tracking, and dataflow settings together, that a caller schedules an actual satellite contact against.
aws_guard_duty_detector: `aws_guard_duty_detector` turns on GuardDuty for an account and Region, the real, top-level resource that continuously analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail events for threats, every other GuardDuty resource, filters, IP lists, member associations, attaches to a detector.
aws_guard_duty_filter: `aws_guard_duty_filter` automatically suppresses or auto-archives real findings matching a defined criteria from an `aws_guard_duty_detector`, cutting down alert noise from findings a caller has already determined aren't actionable.
aws_guard_duty_ipset: `aws_guard_duty_ipset` is a real, trusted list of IP addresses an `aws_guard_duty_detector` never generates findings against, for a caller's own known-safe scanners or internal tools that would otherwise look like malicious activity.
aws_guard_duty_malware_protection_plan: `aws_guard_duty_malware_protection_plan` automatically scans real objects uploaded to a specific S3 bucket for malware the moment they land, GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3, independent of `aws_guard_duty_detector`'s own network- and log-based threat detection.
aws_guard_duty_member: `aws_guard_duty_member` associates another real AWS account's own `aws_guard_duty_detector` as a member under an administrator account, so a security team can view and manage GuardDuty findings across every member account from one central place.
aws_guard_duty_publishing_destination: `aws_guard_duty_publishing_destination` exports an `aws_guard_duty_detector`'s own findings continuously to a real S3 bucket, for long-term retention or for feeding a caller's own SIEM rather than only viewing findings in the GuardDuty console.
aws_guard_duty_threat_entity_set: `aws_guard_duty_threat_entity_set` is GuardDuty's newer, broader entity list, IP addresses, domain names, and SHA-256 file hashes together rather than IP addresses alone, that an `aws_guard_duty_detector` generates findings against, GuardDuty's recommended replacement for the IP-only `aws_guard_duty_threat_intel_set`. Introduced September 2025.
aws_guard_duty_threat_intel_set: `aws_guard_duty_threat_intel_set` is a real, custom list of known-malicious IP addresses that an `aws_guard_duty_detector` generates findings against, extending GuardDuty's own built-in threat intelligence with a caller's own data.
aws_guard_duty_trusted_entity_set: `aws_guard_duty_trusted_entity_set` is GuardDuty's newer, broader trusted list, covering domains as well as IP addresses, that an `aws_guard_duty_detector` never generates findings against, GuardDuty's recommended replacement for the IP-only `aws_guard_duty_ipset`. Introduced September 2025.
aws_health_imaging_datastore: `aws_health_imaging_datastore` is the real, central repository AWS HealthImaging stores medical imaging data in, DICOM P10 files imported from S3 and transformed into image sets of metadata and pixel-data image frames, built for petabyte-scale, subsecond image retrieval.
aws_health_lake_data_transformation_prof: `aws_health_lake_data_transformation_profile` defines the real, AI-assisted mapping rules HealthLake's Data Transformation Agent uses to convert legacy healthcare data, C-CDA documents or relational data, into FHIR R4 resources, created as a mutable draft and promoted to an immutable, published version once ready. Announced in preview in March 2026, genuinely new enough that this session verified it live rather than trusting a remembered description.
aws_health_lake_fhirdatastore: `aws_health_lake_fhirdatastore` creates a real, managed, FHIR R4-compliant datastore that AWS HealthLake stores and indexes structured health data in, queryable directly through the FHIR API rather than a caller building their own FHIR server.
aws_iam_access_key: `aws_iam_access_key` issues a real, long-lived programmatic credential, an access key ID and secret, for an `aws_iam_user`, the actual credential used for CLI and SDK calls made as that user rather than through a browser session.
aws_iam_group: `aws_iam_group` creates a real, named collection of IAM users, letting a caller attach a policy once to the group and have it apply to every current and future user added to it, rather than attaching the same policy to each user individually.
aws_iam_instance_profile: `aws_iam_instance_profile` wraps an `aws_iam_role` in the real container EC2 actually requires to attach that role's permissions to a running instance, an instance can't assume a role directly without one.
aws_iam_managed_policy: `aws_iam_managed_policy` creates a real, standalone, reusable IAM policy document that can be attached to many users, groups, and roles at once, and updated in one place to change permissions everywhere it's attached, AWS's own recommended alternative to an inline policy embedded directly in a single identity.
aws_iam_oidcprovider: `aws_iam_oidcprovider` establishes real trust between IAM and an external OpenID Connect identity provider, GitHub Actions or an EKS cluster's own OIDC issuer among common ones, so an `aws_iam_role` can be assumed directly using that provider's tokens instead of a long-lived IAM credential.
aws_iam_policy:
`aws_iam_policy` creates a standalone, reusable IAM policy, a real JSON
document describing what's allowed. It grants nothing on its own,
attach it to a role or user with `aws_iam_role_policy_attachment` to
actually apply it.
aws_iam_role:
An IAM role grants a set of permissions to whatever's allowed to assume
it, an EC2 instance, a Lambda function, another AWS account. `aws_iam_role`
creates the role and its trust policy, real permissions are attached
separately, via `aws_iam_role_policy_attachment`.
aws_iam_role_policy_attachment:
`aws_iam_role_policy_attachment` is the actual grant, it attaches an
existing, standalone policy to an existing role. Neither the role nor
the policy alone grants anything, this attachment is what connects
them.
aws_iam_samlprovider: `aws_iam_samlprovider` establishes real trust between IAM and an external SAML 2.0 identity provider, a corporate Active Directory Federation Services setup, for instance, so a workforce user can federate into an `aws_iam_role` using their existing enterprise credentials rather than a separate IAM identity.
aws_iam_server_certificate: `aws_iam_server_certificate` uploads a real X.509 certificate and private key to IAM for use with a Classic Load Balancer or CloudFront, IAM's original, legacy certificate storage from before AWS Certificate Manager existed to handle this instead.
aws_iam_user: `aws_iam_user` creates a real, individual IAM identity, distinct from an `aws_iam_role`, meant for a long-lived person or application that needs its own durable credentials rather than assuming temporary ones.
aws_iam_user_to_group_addition: `aws_iam_user_to_group_addition` is the real, actual membership grant adding an `aws_iam_user` to an `aws_iam_group`. Neither existing alone makes a user a group member, this addition is what connects them.
aws_iam_virtual_mfadevice: `aws_iam_virtual_mfadevice` registers a real, software-based MFA device, an authenticator app rather than a physical hardware token, that gets assigned to an `aws_iam_user` or the account root user to require a second factor at sign-in.
aws_image_builder_container_recipe: `aws_image_builder_container_recipe` defines the real base container image and the ordered build and test components applied to it, that an `aws_image_builder_image_pipeline` runs to actually produce a new container image, the container-image counterpart to `aws_image_builder_image_recipe`.
aws_image_builder_distribution_configura: `aws_image_builder_distribution_configuration` defines which real Regions and accounts an `aws_image_builder_image_pipeline`'s output gets copied and shared to once built, rather than a caller manually copying a new AMI everywhere it's needed.
aws_image_builder_image: `aws_image_builder_image` is the real, actual output, an AMI or container image, produced by running an `aws_image_builder_image_pipeline` once, either on its own recurring schedule or triggered manually.
aws_image_builder_image_pipeline: `aws_image_builder_image_pipeline` automates the recurring build, test, and distribution of a real machine image or container image, combining an `aws_image_builder_image_recipe` or `aws_image_builder_container_recipe` with build infrastructure and an `aws_image_builder_distribution_configuration` into one scheduled, repeatable process.
aws_image_builder_image_recipe: `aws_image_builder_image_recipe` defines the real base AMI and the ordered build and test components applied to it, that an `aws_image_builder_image_pipeline` runs to actually produce a new, hardened, updated AMI.
aws_image_builder_lifecycle_policy: `aws_image_builder_lifecycle_policy` automatically deprecates or deletes an `aws_image_builder_image_pipeline`'s older real output images on a defined schedule, real cleanup that keeps old, unpatched AMIs from accumulating indefinitely.
aws_inspector_assessment_target: `aws_inspector_assessment_target` defined a real, tag-based group of EC2 instances that an `aws_inspector_assessment_template` ran a security assessment against, in Amazon Inspector Classic, the original architecture Amazon Inspector shipped with. Inspector Classic is no longer available to new accounts, or to accounts that haven't run an assessment in the last 6 months, and reaches full end of support on May 20, 2026; the redesigned Amazon Inspector (Inspector v2) is the current, actively developed service.
aws_inspector_assessment_template: `aws_inspector_assessment_template` defined the real rules packages and duration for a security assessment run against an `aws_inspector_assessment_target` in Amazon Inspector Classic. Reaches full end of support May 20, 2026, alongside the rest of Inspector Classic.
aws_inspector_resource_group: `aws_inspector_resource_group` was the real, tag-based filter defining exactly which EC2 instances belonged to an `aws_inspector_assessment_target` in Amazon Inspector Classic. Reaches full end of support May 20, 2026, alongside the rest of Inspector Classic.
aws_inspector_v2_cis_scan_configuration: `aws_inspector_v2_cis_scan_configuration` schedules real, recurring CIS benchmark compliance scans against EC2 instances, checking actual operating-system configuration against a defined CIS standard rather than the vulnerability scanning Inspector v2 otherwise focuses on.
aws_inspector_v2_code_security_integrati: `aws_inspector_v2_code_security_integration` connects Amazon Inspector to a real source-code platform, GitHub or GitLab, so Inspector's Code Security capability can scan up to 100,000 real repositories' default branches for vulnerabilities directly in the source, shifting detection left of a deployed, running resource. Launched June 2025.
aws_inspector_v2_code_security_scan_conf: `aws_inspector_v2_code_security_scan_configuration` defines real scanning rules, applied by default to every new repository or scoped to specific ones by tag, under an `aws_inspector_v2_code_security_integration`, up to three default configurations per project.
aws_inspector_v2_connector: `aws_inspector_v2_connector` is the real, account-level connection Amazon Inspector's Code Security capability uses to reach a specific source-code provider account, the resource an `aws_inspector_v2_code_security_integration` is actually built on top of.
aws_inspector_v2_filter: `aws_inspector_v2_filter` suppresses, or routes to a specific notification, real Inspector v2 findings matching defined criteria, severity, resource type, package name, cutting down alert noise from findings a caller has already triaged or determined aren't actionable.
aws_instance: `aws_instance` launches a real, virtual server, an EC2 instance, in the AWS Cloud, its instance type determining the actual balance of compute, memory, network, and storage hardware available to it. It's the single most fundamental EC2 resource, the one an AMI, a key pair, a security group, and an EBS volume all ultimately attach to or run on.
aws_interconnect_connection: `aws_interconnect_connection` (AWS::DirectConnect::Interconnect) is a real, physical connection, over standard Ethernet fiber, between an AWS Direct Connect Partner's own network and a Direct Connect location, that the partner uses to provision and resell hosted Direct Connect connections to their own customers, rather than each customer needing a direct physical link to AWS themselves.
aws_internet_gateway: `aws_internet_gateway` is a real, horizontally scaled, redundant VPC component that allows communication between resources in a VPC and the internet, the actual resource an `aws_route` with a 0.0.0.0/0 destination points traffic at for a subnet to be genuinely public.
aws_internet_monitor_monitor: `aws_internet_monitor_monitor` uses AWS's own global networking data, cross-referenced against a defined set of resources, VPCs, CloudFront distributions, WorkSpaces, to continuously measure real internet performance and availability between an application and its actual end users, and alert on regional disruptions or unusual latency without a caller needing external synthetic monitoring.
aws_invoicing_invoice_unit: `aws_invoicing_invoice_unit` groups a real, mutually exclusive set of member accounts into one business entity, a subsidiary, a legal entity, a cost center, so AWS issues that entity its own separate invoice rather than one combined invoice for an entire AWS Organization. Reached general availability December 2024.
aws_io_t_account_audit_configuration: `aws_io_t_account_audit_configuration` turns on AWS IoT Device Defender's real, account-wide audit checks, security-related misconfigurations across an account's things, certificates, and policies, that an `aws_io_t_scheduled_audit` then runs on a recurring basis.
aws_io_t_authorizer: `aws_io_t_authorizer` runs a real, caller-defined Lambda function to authenticate and authorize a device's connection using a custom token scheme, rather than the X.509 certificate model `aws_io_t_certificate` and `aws_io_t_policy` provide.
aws_io_t_billing_group: `aws_io_t_billing_group` organizes real `aws_io_t_thing`s for cost allocation and tracking purposes, kept separate from an `aws_io_t_thing_group`'s own operational grouping.
aws_io_t_cacertificate: `aws_io_t_cacertificate` registers a real, caller-owned certificate authority with AWS IoT, so device certificates the caller's own CA issues, rather than only ones AWS IoT itself issues, can be trusted to authenticate an `aws_io_t_thing`'s connection.
aws_io_t_certificate: `aws_io_t_certificate` is a real X.509 certificate AWS IoT issues or registers for device authentication, the actual credential an `aws_io_t_thing` presents to authenticate its MQTT or HTTPS connection to AWS IoT Core.
aws_io_t_certificate_provider: `aws_io_t_certificate_provider` runs a real, caller-defined Lambda function during Fleet Provisioning to issue a device's `aws_io_t_certificate` dynamically, using a custom or third-party CA, rather than relying only on AWS IoT's own certificate issuance.
aws_io_t_command: `aws_io_t_command` defines a real, reusable, named remote command with its own custom payload schema, that AWS IoT Device Management Commands sends to a targeted device and tracks execution status for, without a caller managing MQTT topics, payload formats, or status tracking by hand. Reached general availability November 2024.
aws_io_t_custom_metric: `aws_io_t_custom_metric` defines a real, caller-specific metric, beyond AWS IoT's own built-in ones, that a device reports and an `aws_io_t_security_profile` can evaluate as part of Device Defender's behavioral detection.
aws_io_t_dimension: `aws_io_t_dimension` scopes an `aws_io_t_security_profile`'s own behavior checks to a real, defined subset, a specific set of MQTT topics, for instance, rather than the profile applying uniformly across everything a device does.
aws_io_t_domain_configuration: `aws_io_t_domain_configuration` lets devices connect to AWS IoT Core over a real, custom domain name and TLS configuration instead of the default AWS-provided IoT endpoint.
aws_io_t_encryption_configuration: `aws_io_t_encryption_configuration` sets a real, caller-managed KMS key that AWS IoT Core uses to encrypt data at rest account-wide, in place of AWS's own default encryption key.
aws_io_t_fleet_metric: `aws_io_t_fleet_metric` aggregates a real CloudWatch metric across every device in an `aws_io_t_thing_group`, fleet-wide visibility, average battery level across a whole product line, for instance, rather than only per-device metrics.
aws_io_t_job: `aws_io_t_job` defines a real, remote operation, a firmware update, a config change, a reboot command, deployed to and tracked across one or more real `aws_io_t_thing`s or `aws_io_t_thing_group`s, with per-device execution status reported back to AWS IoT.
aws_io_t_job_template: `aws_io_t_job_template` is a real, reusable configuration, rollout rate, timeout, abort criteria, that an `aws_io_t_job` can be created from, so the same recurring job shape doesn't need to be configured from scratch every time.
aws_io_t_logging: `aws_io_t_logging` configures real, account-wide CloudWatch Logs delivery for AWS IoT Core activity, connection attempts, rule executions, errors, at a defined verbosity level.
aws_io_t_mitigation_action: `aws_io_t_mitigation_action` defines a real, automated remediation, revoking a certificate, adding a device to a quarantine thing group, that an `aws_io_t_scheduled_audit`'s findings can trigger automatically rather than requiring a human to act on every audit finding.
aws_io_t_policy: `aws_io_t_policy` is a real, JSON-based document defining exactly which MQTT topics and AWS IoT actions a connected device is actually allowed to publish, subscribe to, or invoke, attached to an `aws_io_t_certificate` through an `aws_io_t_policy_principal_attachment`.
aws_io_t_policy_principal_attachment: `aws_io_t_policy_principal_attachment` is the real, actual grant attaching an `aws_io_t_policy` to a specific certificate or other principal. A policy with nothing attached to it authorizes no real device's connection.
aws_io_t_provisioning_template: `aws_io_t_provisioning_template` defines the real resources, an `aws_io_t_thing`, a certificate, policy attachments, that AWS IoT Fleet Provisioning automatically creates the first time a new device connects, so a device can be manufactured with generic bootstrap credentials rather than a unique certificate burned in at the factory.
aws_io_t_role_alias: `aws_io_t_role_alias` lets a real, authenticated device exchange its `aws_io_t_certificate` for temporary AWS credentials tied to a specific IAM role, through the IoT credentials provider, without embedding a long-lived AWS access key on the device itself.
aws_io_t_scheduled_audit: `aws_io_t_scheduled_audit` runs Device Defender's real, configured audit checks on a recurring schedule, defined by an `aws_io_t_account_audit_configuration`, real, ongoing compliance checking rather than a one-time manual review.
aws_io_t_security_profile: `aws_io_t_security_profile` defines real, expected behavior for a group of devices, connection frequency, message size, authorization failures, that Device Defender's Detect capability continuously measures live device behavior against, alerting when a device deviates from its own defined profile.
aws_io_t_software_package: `aws_io_t_software_package` is a real, named entry in the AWS IoT Software Package Catalog, an inventory of firmware, OS updates, or applications, whose `aws_io_t_software_package_version`s get associated with things and deployed through an `aws_io_t_job`. Reached general availability in 2023.
aws_io_t_software_package_version: `aws_io_t_software_package_version` is one real, specific, deployable version, a set of actual files, firmware, configuration, security patches, of an `aws_io_t_software_package`.
aws_io_t_stream: `aws_io_t_stream` delivers a real, large file, a firmware image, in ordered chunks over MQTT to a device running an `aws_io_t_job`, AWS IoT's own mechanism for file delivery to devices that can't make a normal HTTPS download request.
aws_io_t_thing: `aws_io_t_thing` registers a real device or logical entity in the AWS IoT registry, the actual identity an `aws_io_t_certificate` gets attached to and an `aws_io_t_policy` ultimately governs the permissions of.
aws_io_t_thing_group: `aws_io_t_thing_group` is a real, static or dynamic (query-based) collection of `aws_io_t_thing`s, the actual grouping an `aws_io_t_job` or `aws_io_t_fleet_metric` targets rather than every operation addressing individual things one at a time.
aws_io_t_thing_principal_attachment: `aws_io_t_thing_principal_attachment` is the real, actual link between an `aws_io_t_thing` and its `aws_io_t_certificate`. A certificate with no thing attachment can still authenticate an MQTT connection but has no thing identity behind it.
aws_io_t_thing_type: `aws_io_t_thing_type` defines a real, reusable template of common attributes and searchable metadata for a category of `aws_io_t_thing`s, temperature sensors versus door locks, for instance, rather than every thing's attributes being defined from scratch.
aws_io_t_topic_rule: `aws_io_t_topic_rule` is a real, SQL-like rule the AWS IoT Rules Engine evaluates against every message published to a matching MQTT topic, routing matching messages to a real target, Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, an `aws_io_tanalytics_channel`, and dozens of other AWS services.
aws_io_t_topic_rule_destination: `aws_io_t_topic_rule_destination` registers a real HTTPS endpoint an `aws_io_t_topic_rule` can send matched messages to, requiring the endpoint to confirm ownership before AWS IoT will actually deliver any traffic to it.
aws_io_tanalytics_channel: `aws_io_tanalytics_channel` is the real entry point AWS IoT Analytics ingests raw device messages into, typically fed directly by an `aws_io_t_topic_rule`, and holds the unprocessed data an `aws_io_tanalytics_pipeline` reads from.
aws_io_tanalytics_dataset: `aws_io_tanalytics_dataset` runs a real, recurring SQL query or containerized analysis against an `aws_io_tanalytics_datastore` and materializes the result, the actual output a caller or downstream application reads insights from.
aws_io_tanalytics_datastore: `aws_io_tanalytics_datastore` holds the real, processed output of an `aws_io_tanalytics_pipeline`, the actual data an `aws_io_tanalytics_dataset`'s query or container runs against.
aws_io_tanalytics_pipeline: `aws_io_tanalytics_pipeline` is a real, ordered sequence of activities, filtering, enriching, transforming, that processes messages from an `aws_io_tanalytics_channel` and writes the result into an `aws_io_tanalytics_datastore`.
aws_io_tcore_device_advisor_suite_defini: `aws_io_tcore_device_advisor_suite_definition` defines a real, pre-built or custom test suite that validates a device's software against AWS IoT Core's own best practices, connection reliability, MQTT compliance, before that device ships to production, catching real integration issues in a controlled test environment rather than in the field.
aws_io_tevents_alarm_model: `aws_io_tevents_alarm_model` is a real, pre-built alarm pattern, built on the same underlying state-machine mechanism as an `aws_io_tevents_detector_model`, purpose-built for the common case of a threshold-based alarm rather than a caller designing a full custom state machine for it.
aws_io_tevents_detector_model: `aws_io_tevents_detector_model` is a real state machine, defined states and the events that transition between them, that AWS IoT Events runs one instance of per real, tracked entity, an individual piece of equipment, a process, evaluating incoming data against it continuously to detect real operational states like a stuck valve or an overheating motor.
aws_io_tevents_input: `aws_io_tevents_input` defines the real message attributes an `aws_io_tevents_detector_model` actually evaluates, the structured data a detector model's states and transitions are written in terms of.
aws_io_tfleet_wise_campaign: `aws_io_tfleet_wise_campaign` defines real, specific data collection rules, which signals, at what rate, under what trigger condition, deployed to an `aws_io_tfleet_wise_vehicle` or `aws_io_tfleet_wise_fleet`'s own Edge Agent. aws_io_tfleet_wise_decoder_manifest: `aws_io_tfleet_wise_decoder_manifest` translates a real vehicle's raw CAN bus or OBD messages into the named signals an `aws_io_tfleet_wise_model_manifest` defines, the actual decoding logic the Edge Agent applies on the vehicle itself. aws_io_tfleet_wise_fleet: `aws_io_tfleet_wise_fleet` is a real, logical grouping of `aws_io_tfleet_wise_vehicle`s that an `aws_io_tfleet_wise_campaign` can target together rather than every vehicle being addressed individually. Part of AWS IoT FleetWise, which is no longer open to new customers.
aws_io_tfleet_wise_model_manifest: `aws_io_tfleet_wise_model_manifest` selects the real, specific signals from an `aws_io_tfleet_wise_signal_catalog` that apply to one vehicle model, the actual signal set an `aws_io_tfleet_wise_vehicle` of that model can report. Part of AWS IoT FleetWise, which is no longer open to new customers.
aws_io_tfleet_wise_signal_catalog: `aws_io_tfleet_wise_signal_catalog` is a real, comprehensive catalog of every vehicle signal, engine RPM, door status, that an `aws_io_tfleet_wise_model_manifest` selects a relevant subset from for one specific vehicle model. Part of AWS IoT FleetWise, which is no longer open to new customers.
aws_io_tfleet_wise_state_template: `aws_io_tfleet_wise_state_template` tracks a real, defined set of signals' current state on a vehicle, reported on change or on a periodic interval by the Edge Agent, distinct from an `aws_io_tfleet_wise_campaign`'s own bulk data-collection model. Part of AWS IoT FleetWise, which is no longer open to new customers.
aws_io_tfleet_wise_vehicle: `aws_io_tfleet_wise_vehicle` registers a real, individual vehicle running the AWS IoT FleetWise Edge Agent, the actual entity an `aws_io_tfleet_wise_campaign` and `aws_io_tfleet_wise_state_template` get associated with to collect data from. aws_io_tsite_wise_asset: `aws_io_tsite_wise_asset` represents one real, physical piece of industrial equipment, created from an `aws_io_tsite_wise_asset_model`, that an `aws_io_tsite_wise_gateway` streams real, live sensor data into.
aws_io_tsite_wise_asset_model: `aws_io_tsite_wise_asset_model` is a real, reusable template defining the properties, hierarchy, and computed metrics common to a category of equipment, a wind turbine model, for instance, that every `aws_io_tsite_wise_asset` created from it automatically inherits.
aws_io_tsite_wise_computation_model: `aws_io_tsite_wise_computation_model` defines a real, reusable computation, a transform, metric, or anomaly-detection model, that binds to asset or asset-model properties through a named data-binding configuration, so the same calculation logic can be shared and applied consistently across `aws_io_tsite_wise_asset_model`s rather than redefined inside each one individually. aws_io_tsite_wise_dashboard: `aws_io_tsite_wise_dashboard` is a real, saved visualization, trend charts, KPIs, of `aws_io_tsite_wise_asset` data inside an `aws_io_tsite_wise_project`.
aws_io_tsite_wise_dataset: `aws_io_tsite_wise_dataset` links a real, external structured dataset, maintenance records, work orders, to `aws_io_tsite_wise_asset` data, so operational context beyond raw sensor readings can be queried and visualized alongside it.
aws_io_tsite_wise_gateway: `aws_io_tsite_wise_gateway` is real, on-premises software that collects data from industrial protocols, OPC-UA among them, and streams it into an `aws_io_tsite_wise_asset`'s properties, the actual bridge between a factory floor and SiteWise's own cloud-based asset model.
aws_io_tsite_wise_portal: `aws_io_tsite_wise_portal` is a real, managed web application, with its own users and access control, through which SiteWise data actually gets visualized, the container an `aws_io_tsite_wise_project` and its dashboards live inside.
aws_io_tsite_wise_project: `aws_io_tsite_wise_project` groups a real set of `aws_io_tsite_wise_asset`s and `aws_io_tsite_wise_dashboard`s inside an `aws_io_tsite_wise_portal`, organizing what a specific team or use case actually sees when they open the portal.
aws_io_tthings_graph_flow_template: `aws_io_tthings_graph_flow_template` defined a real, visual workflow connecting multiple devices and services together in AWS IoT Things Graph. AWS IoT Things Graph was fully discontinued and transitioned to AWS IoT TwinMaker on November 9, 2022; its APIs are deprecated, kept only for backward compatibility, and should not be used for new work.
aws_io_ttwin_maker_component_type: `aws_io_ttwin_maker_component_type` is a real, reusable definition of properties and behavior, a temperature sensor's own data schema, for instance, that an `aws_io_ttwin_maker_entity` in an `aws_io_ttwin_maker_workspace` can be built from.
aws_io_ttwin_maker_entity: `aws_io_ttwin_maker_entity` is the real, digital representation of one physical object, a specific machine, a room, built from one or more `aws_io_ttwin_maker_component_type`s inside an `aws_io_ttwin_maker_workspace`.
aws_io_ttwin_maker_scene: `aws_io_ttwin_maker_scene` composes a real, 3D visualization of an `aws_io_ttwin_maker_workspace`'s own entities, tagging real-time data onto a 3D model rather than only viewing entity data as raw numbers.
aws_io_ttwin_maker_sync_job: `aws_io_ttwin_maker_sync_job` keeps an `aws_io_ttwin_maker_workspace`'s own entities automatically synchronized with a real, external source of truth, so a digital twin doesn't drift out of date with the physical or logical system it represents.
aws_io_ttwin_maker_workspace: `aws_io_ttwin_maker_workspace` is the real, top-level AWS IoT TwinMaker container an `aws_io_ttwin_maker_entity`, `aws_io_ttwin_maker_component_type`, and `aws_io_ttwin_maker_scene` all belong to, the digital twin project every other TwinMaker resource is scoped inside.
aws_io_twireless_destination: `aws_io_twireless_destination` routes a real, decoded LoRaWAN or Sidewalk message from an `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device` to an `aws_io_t_topic_rule`, the actual bridge from AWS IoT Wireless into the rest of AWS IoT Core.
aws_io_twireless_device_profile: `aws_io_twireless_device_profile` is a real, reusable template of LoRaWAN device capabilities, supported data rates, class type, applied to an `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device` rather than every device's radio characteristics being configured individually.
aws_io_twireless_fuota_task: `aws_io_twireless_fuota_task` runs a real firmware-update-over-the-air campaign across a group of LoRaWAN `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device`s, using multicast delivery to update many devices' firmware efficiently rather than one at a time.
aws_io_twireless_multicast_group: `aws_io_twireless_multicast_group` sends the real, same LoRaWAN downlink message to a defined group of `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device`s at once, rather than a caller addressing every device in the group individually.
aws_io_twireless_network_analyzer_config: `aws_io_twireless_network_analyzer_configuration` defines a real, live traffic-tracing session scoped to specific `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device`s or gateways, for debugging LoRaWAN connectivity issues as they actually happen rather than after the fact from logs alone.
aws_io_twireless_partner_account: `aws_io_twireless_partner_account` links a real Amazon Sidewalk partner account to AWS IoT Wireless, required before a caller's own Sidewalk `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device`s can be managed through the service.
aws_io_twireless_service_profile: `aws_io_twireless_service_profile` is a real, reusable template of LoRaWAN network server behavior, applied to an `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device` alongside its own `aws_io_twireless_device_profile`.
aws_io_twireless_task_definition: `aws_io_twireless_task_definition` is the real, reusable firmware update definition, the actual image and update parameters, that an `aws_io_twireless_fuota_task` deploys.
aws_io_twireless_wireless_device: `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device` registers a real, individual LoRaWAN or Amazon Sidewalk device with AWS IoT Wireless, the actual endpoint that connects through an `aws_io_twireless_wireless_gateway` to AWS IoT Core.
aws_io_twireless_wireless_device_import_: `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device_import_task` bulk-imports real Sidewalk devices from a manufacturer-provided list into AWS IoT Wireless as `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device`s, rather than a caller registering each device one at a time.
aws_io_twireless_wireless_gateway: `aws_io_twireless_wireless_gateway` registers a real LoRaWAN gateway, the physical radio hardware that receives transmissions from an `aws_io_twireless_wireless_device` and forwards them to AWS IoT Wireless.
aws_ivs_channel: `aws_ivs_channel` is the real, core Amazon IVS resource a broadcaster streams video into and viewers watch from, with its own ingest endpoint, playback URL, and configurable latency mode.
aws_ivs_encoder_configuration: `aws_ivs_encoder_configuration` sets real encoding parameters, resolution, bitrate, for Amazon IVS Real-Time Streaming, applied to participants in an `aws_ivs_stage` rather than a single broadcast `aws_ivs_channel`.
aws_ivs_ingest_configuration: `aws_ivs_ingest_configuration` specifies a real, named ingest protocol, RTMP or RTMPS, for broadcasting into a specific `aws_ivs_stage`'s real-time stage, including whether insecure RTMP ingest is allowed and an optional customer-assigned user ID used to link the ingest participant to the customer's own systems. Verified live against AWS's own CloudFormation reference this session, resolving last session's flagged, unverified version of this entry.
aws_ivs_playback_key_pair: `aws_ivs_playback_key_pair` signs real, private playback tokens for an `aws_ivs_channel` configured to require authorization, restricting viewing to clients that present a token signed by this specific key pair.
aws_ivs_playback_restriction_policy: `aws_ivs_playback_restriction_policy` restricts real playback of an `aws_ivs_channel` by geography or origin domain, blocking viewers outside an allowed country list or a site that isn't the caller's own from embedding the stream.
aws_ivs_public_key: `aws_ivs_public_key` registers a real public key IVS validates participant tokens for an `aws_ivs_stage` against, the Real-Time Streaming counterpart to `aws_ivs_playback_key_pair`'s own channel-playback authorization.
aws_ivs_recording_configuration: `aws_ivs_recording_configuration` automatically records an `aws_ivs_channel`'s live stream to a real S3 bucket as it broadcasts, so a stream is available for on-demand playback after it ends without a caller building their own recording pipeline.
aws_ivs_stage: `aws_ivs_stage` is Amazon IVS's real, low-latency, multi-participant video collaboration resource, up to several hosts and guests interacting live together, distinct from an `aws_ivs_channel`'s own single-broadcaster-to-many-viewers model.
aws_ivs_storage_configuration: `aws_ivs_storage_configuration` defines a real S3 destination that an `aws_ivs_stage`'s own composite recording gets written to, the stage counterpart to `aws_ivs_recording_configuration`'s channel-level recording.
aws_ivs_stream_key: `aws_ivs_stream_key` is the real, secret credential streaming software uses to authenticate and publish video to a specific `aws_ivs_channel`, distinct from the channel's own public ingest endpoint URL.
aws_ivschat_logging_configuration: `aws_ivschat_logging_configuration` streams a real `aws_ivschat_room`'s chat messages to a destination, CloudWatch Logs, Kinesis Data Firehose, or S3, for moderation review or analytics rather than messages existing only transiently in the room.
aws_ivschat_room: `aws_ivschat_room` creates a real, managed chat room, typically paired alongside an `aws_ivs_channel`'s live stream, that Amazon IVS Chat handles message fan-out, moderation, and connection scaling for.
aws_kafka_connect_connector: `aws_kafka_connect_connector` runs a real, managed Kafka Connect connector, MSK Connect provisioning and scaling the underlying compute, moving data between an Apache Kafka or Amazon MSK cluster and an external system without a caller operating their own Kafka Connect worker cluster.
aws_kafka_connect_custom_plugin: `aws_kafka_connect_custom_plugin` uploads the real connector code, a JDBC sink, an S3 source, that an `aws_kafka_connect_connector` actually runs, MSK Connect's own way of using a connector implementation that isn't AWS-provided.
aws_kafka_connect_worker_configuration: `aws_kafka_connect_worker_configuration` sets real Kafka Connect worker-level properties applied to an `aws_kafka_connect_connector`'s own underlying runtime, beyond the connector's specific configuration alone.
aws_kendra_data_source: `aws_kendra_data_source` connects a real content repository, S3, SharePoint, Confluence, a website, to an `aws_kendra_index`, so Kendra can crawl and index its content rather than a caller uploading documents by hand.
aws_kendra_faq: `aws_kendra_faq` loads a real, structured set of question-and-answer pairs directly into an `aws_kendra_index`, so an exact FAQ match can be surfaced with high confidence rather than relying only on Kendra's own document-search relevance.
aws_kendra_index: `aws_kendra_index` is the real, core Amazon Kendra search index, built from one or more `aws_kendra_data_source`s, that a caller's own natural-language search queries actually run against.
aws_kendra_query_suggestions_block_list: `aws_kendra_query_suggestions_block_list` blocks specific real terms from appearing in an `aws_kendra_index`'s own autocomplete query suggestions, without removing the underlying documents that contain them from search results entirely.
aws_kendra_ranking_execution_plan: `aws_kendra_ranking_execution_plan` provisions Kendra Intelligent Ranking, a real, standalone semantic re-ranking API a caller applies to results from their own separate search system, OpenSearch or Elasticsearch, for instance, independent of using a full `aws_kendra_index`.
aws_kendra_thesaurus: `aws_kendra_thesaurus` teaches an `aws_kendra_index` real synonym relationships, so a search for one term also matches documents using an equivalent term, improving recall beyond exact keyword matching.
aws_key_pair: `aws_key_pair` creates or imports a real SSH key pair, AWS storing the public key and the caller keeping the private key, used to securely retrieve an `aws_instance`'s initial administrator password or authenticate an SSH connection to it.
aws_kinesis_analytics_application: `aws_kinesis_analytics_application` runs a real, continuous SQL query directly against a streaming data source, Kinesis Data Streams or Firehose, the original, SQL-based Kinesis Data Analytics application type, distinct from the newer Apache Flink-based Kinesis Data Analytics v2 applications.
aws_kinesis_analytics_application_output: `aws_kinesis_analytics_application_output` defines a real destination, another Kinesis stream, a Lambda function, that an `aws_kinesis_analytics_application`'s own continuous SQL query results actually get delivered to.
aws_kinesis_analytics_application_refere: `aws_kinesis_analytics_application_reference_data_source` adds a real static reference table, loaded from an S3 object, that an `aws_kinesis_analytics_application`'s SQL can join against incoming stream records. This is scoped to the original SQL-based Kinesis Data Analytics application type, which AWS has fully discontinued: no new applications could be created after October 15, 2025, and all remaining applications were deleted and support ended on January 27, 2026, a date now in the past. The distinct, current generation is `aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application`, built on Apache Flink.
aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application: `aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application` runs a real Apache Flink stream-processing application, or an interactive Kinesis Data Analytics Studio notebook when its mode is set to INTERACTIVE, distinct from the now-discontinued SQL-based Kinesis Data Analytics application type this v2 generation replaced.
aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application_clo: `aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application_cloud_watch_logging_option` attaches a real CloudWatch log stream to an `aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application`, so the Flink application's own runtime logs land somewhere durable and queryable rather than being discarded.
aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application_out: `aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application_output` adds a real external destination, a Kinesis data stream, a Firehose delivery stream, or a Lambda function, that an `aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application` writes its processed results to.
aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application_ref: `aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application_reference_data_source` adds a real static reference table, loaded from an S3 object, that an `aws_kinesis_analytics_v2_application`'s SQL-based code can join against incoming stream records.
aws_kinesis_firehose_delivery_stream: `aws_kinesis_firehose_delivery_stream` creates a real managed pipeline that acquires, transforms, and delivers streaming data within seconds to a destination such as S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, or a third-party analytics tool. AWS renamed the underlying service from "Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose" to "Amazon Data Firehose" in February 2024; the resource name and behavior are unchanged.
aws_kinesis_stream: `aws_kinesis_stream` creates a real, sharded data stream that ingests and retains streaming records for a configurable window, from the default 24 hours up to 365 days, for real-time, multi-consumer processing.
aws_kinesis_stream_consumer: `aws_kinesis_stream_consumer` registers a real dedicated-throughput consumer on an `aws_kinesis_stream` using enhanced fan-out, so this one consumer gets its own 2 MB/sec-per-shard read pipe instead of sharing the stream's default throughput with every other reader.
aws_kinesis_video_signaling_channel: `aws_kinesis_video_signaling_channel` creates a real WebRTC signaling channel that exchanges the SDP offers/answers and ICE candidates needed to establish a peer-to-peer media connection between WebRTC clients, distinct from `aws_kinesis_video_stream`'s own role storing and replaying the actual media.
aws_kinesis_video_stream: `aws_kinesis_video_stream` creates a real stream that captures, stores, and indexes live video and other time-encoded data for playback and downstream analysis.
aws_kms_key: `aws_kms_key` creates a real cryptographic key in AWS Key Management Service, symmetric encryption keys, asymmetric encryption or signing keys, or symmetric HMAC keys, and can create the multi-Region primary key that an `aws_kms_replica_key` replicates from.
