aws_rds_dbinstance: `aws_rds_dbinstance` creates a real managed relational database instance, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, or an Aurora cluster's own compute, the core resource RDS provisions and patches on the customer's behalf.
aws_rds_dbparameter_group: `aws_rds_dbparameter_group` defines a real set of instance-level engine parameters that can be applied to an `aws_rds_dbinstance` instead of hand-tuning the instance individually.
aws_rds_dbproxy: `aws_rds_dbproxy` creates a real, fully managed connection pooler in front of one or more `aws_rds_dbinstance`s or an `aws_rds_dbcluster`, absorbing bursts of application connections without exhausting the database's own native connection limit.
aws_rds_dbproxy_endpoint: `aws_rds_dbproxy_endpoint` adds a real additional, separately addressable endpoint to an `aws_rds_dbproxy`, letting different applications or read/write splits reach the same proxy through different connection strings.
aws_rds_dbproxy_target_group: `aws_rds_dbproxy_target_group` configures a real connection-pooling and failover behavior for the specific `aws_rds_dbcluster` or instances an `aws_rds_dbproxy` routes to.
aws_rds_dbsecurity_group: `aws_rds_dbsecurity_group` was a real access-control mechanism for RDS instances running on the original EC2-Classic network model. EC2-Classic itself was fully retired on August 15, 2023 (AWS's original target date of August 2022 slipped by about a year), so this resource has no functioning target left to attach to; modern RDS deployments use standard VPC security groups instead. This resource describes infrastructure that no longer has anything to provision against, rather than a current option.
aws_rds_dbsecurity_group_ingress: `aws_rds_dbsecurity_group_ingress` added a real ingress rule to an `aws_rds_dbsecurity_group`. Like its parent resource, this targets the EC2-Classic network model, which AWS fully retired on August 15, 2023, so it has no functioning target left to configure.
aws_rds_dbshard_group: `aws_rds_dbshard_group` creates a real DB shard group for Aurora PostgreSQL Limitless Database, distributing a single logical database's write workload across multiple Aurora writer instances contained in the shard group while it's still queried as one database. Aurora Limitless Database reached general availability in 2024, and requires it to already be enabled on the target `aws_rds_dbcluster` before a shard group can be created; only one shard group is allowed per cluster.
aws_rds_dbsnapshot: `aws_rds_dbsnapshot` creates a real point-in-time snapshot of an `aws_rds_dbinstance`, which can later be restored into a new instance.
aws_rds_dbsubnet_group: `aws_rds_dbsubnet_group` defines a real set of VPC subnets that an `aws_rds_dbinstance` or `aws_rds_dbcluster` is allowed to place its network interfaces into.
aws_rds_event_subscription: `aws_rds_event_subscription` subscribes a real SNS topic to receive notifications about events, failovers, backups, parameter changes, occurring on an `aws_rds_dbinstance` or `aws_rds_dbcluster` and related RDS resources.
aws_rds_global_cluster: `aws_rds_global_cluster` creates a real multi-Region Aurora deployment, coordinating a primary `aws_rds_dbcluster` and up to five read-only secondary clusters in other Regions with fast replication and disaster-recovery failover.
aws_rds_integration: `aws_rds_integration` creates a real, zero-ETL integration that continuously replicates an `aws_rds_dbcluster`'s data into Amazon Redshift, so it can be queried for analytics within seconds of being written without a separate extract-load pipeline.
aws_rds_option_group: `aws_rds_option_group` defines a real set of database engine options, such as Oracle's native network encryption or SQL Server's Transparent Data Encryption, that can be enabled on an `aws_rds_dbinstance` beyond what standard engine parameters cover.
aws_redshift_cluster: `aws_redshift_cluster` creates a real, provisioned Amazon Redshift data warehouse cluster, its leader and compute nodes, the original Redshift architecture distinct from the auto-scaling `aws_redshift_serverless_namespace`.
aws_redshift_cluster_parameter_group: `aws_redshift_cluster_parameter_group` defines a real set of engine parameters that can be applied to an `aws_redshift_cluster` instead of hand-tuning the cluster individually.
aws_redshift_cluster_security_group: `aws_redshift_cluster_security_group` was a real access-control mechanism for Redshift clusters running on the original EC2-Classic network model. EC2-Classic itself was fully retired on August 15, 2023, so this resource has no functioning target left to attach to; modern Redshift deployments use standard VPC security groups instead. This resource describes infrastructure that no longer has anything to provision against, rather than a current option.
aws_redshift_cluster_security_group_ingr: `aws_redshift_cluster_security_group_ingress` added a real ingress rule to an `aws_redshift_cluster_security_group`. Like its parent resource, this targets the EC2-Classic network model, which AWS fully retired on August 15, 2023, so it has no functioning target left to configure.
aws_redshift_cluster_subnet_group: `aws_redshift_cluster_subnet_group` defines a real set of VPC subnets that an `aws_redshift_cluster` is allowed to be placed into.
aws_redshift_endpoint_access: `aws_redshift_endpoint_access` creates a real Redshift-managed VPC endpoint that lets clients in a different VPC, or a different account, reach an `aws_redshift_cluster` privately without the cluster's own security group being opened up directly.
aws_redshift_endpoint_authorization: `aws_redshift_endpoint_authorization` grants a real other AWS account permission to create an `aws_redshift_endpoint_access` against this account's `aws_redshift_cluster`, the authorization step that has to happen before the other account's endpoint can be created.
aws_redshift_event_subscription: `aws_redshift_event_subscription` subscribes a real SNS topic to receive notifications about events occurring on an `aws_redshift_cluster`, such as failovers or configuration changes.
aws_redshift_integration: `aws_redshift_integration` creates a real, zero-ETL integration that continuously replicates data from a source such as an RDS or Aurora cluster into Amazon Redshift, so it can be queried for analytics within seconds of being written.
aws_redshift_scheduled_action: `aws_redshift_scheduled_action` schedules a real, recurring Redshift API action, resizing an `aws_redshift_cluster`, pausing it, resuming it, to run automatically on a cron-style schedule rather than being triggered by hand.
aws_redshift_serverless_namespace: `aws_redshift_serverless_namespace` creates a real Redshift Serverless namespace, the collection of database objects, users, and data that automatically scales its own compute, distinct from the manually sized `aws_redshift_cluster`.
aws_redshift_serverless_snapshot: `aws_redshift_serverless_snapshot` creates a real point-in-time snapshot of an `aws_redshift_serverless_namespace`'s data, which can later be restored into a new namespace.
aws_redshift_serverless_workgroup: `aws_redshift_serverless_workgroup` creates a real compute configuration, its capacity in RPUs and network settings, that queries against an `aws_redshift_serverless_namespace` actually run through.
aws_redshift_snapshot_schedule: `aws_redshift_snapshot_schedule` defines a real, recurring cron-style schedule on which an `aws_redshift_cluster` automatically takes snapshots, beyond Redshift's own default automated backups.
aws_refactor_spaces_application: `aws_refactor_spaces_application` registers a real monolith application, its proxy and default route, inside an `aws_refactor_spaces_environment`, the resource that `aws_refactor_spaces_service`s are incrementally carved out of and routed to. Like the rest of Refactor Spaces, this closed to new customers November 7, 2025, with AWS recommending AWS Transform for new work.
aws_refactor_spaces_environment: `aws_refactor_spaces_environment` creates a real top-level container, a shared transit gateway and default settings, that `aws_refactor_spaces_application`s under AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces are organized inside while an application is incrementally strangled apart into microservices. Refactor Spaces closed to new customers on November 7, 2025, a date roughly nine months in the past; existing customers can continue their migrations, with AWS maintaining security and reliability but adding no new features, and pointing new work toward AWS Transform (launched May 2025) instead.
aws_refactor_spaces_service: `aws_refactor_spaces_service` registers a real extracted microservice, and the routing rule that sends its share of an `aws_refactor_spaces_application`'s traffic to it, the mechanism Refactor Spaces uses to migrate traffic incrementally rather than all at once. Like the rest of Refactor Spaces, this closed to new customers November 7, 2025.
aws_rekognition_collection: `aws_rekognition_collection` creates a real container of indexed face vectors that Rekognition's face-search operations compare newly detected faces against, independent of any specific `aws_rekognition_project`.
aws_rekognition_dataset: `aws_rekognition_dataset` imports a real set of labeled training or test images into an `aws_rekognition_project`, the data Custom Labels actually trains and evaluates a model against.
aws_rekognition_project: `aws_rekognition_project` creates a real Rekognition Custom Labels project, the container that groups the `aws_rekognition_dataset`s and trained model versions built to detect a customer's own custom labels rather than Rekognition's built-in label set.
aws_rekognition_stream_processor: `aws_rekognition_stream_processor` creates a real processor that analyzes a live Kinesis video stream in near real time, detecting faces or labels frame by frame and publishing matches, distinct from Rekognition's own batch image and video analysis APIs.
aws_resilience_hub_app: `aws_resilience_hub_app` registers a real application in AWS Resilience Hub, its component resources discovered from CloudFormation, Terraform state, or an EKS cluster, that an `aws_resilience_hub_resiliency_policy` is then assessed against.
aws_resilience_hub_resiliency_policy: `aws_resilience_hub_resiliency_policy` defines real recovery time and recovery point objectives that an `aws_resilience_hub_app` is assessed against, the target Resilience Hub measures the application's actual architecture against to produce a resiliency score.
aws_resilience_hub_v2_policy: `aws_resilience_hub_v2_policy` defines a real, modular, composable resiliency policy under the next-generation AWS Resilience Hub model, reusable and assignable across multiple `aws_resilience_hub_v2_service`s at once rather than one application at a time. This next-generation model, with generative-AI-powered failure mode analysis and organization-wide reporting, launched in May 2026, roughly three months ago, so behavior here is verified live rather than assumed from general knowledge.
aws_resilience_hub_v2_service: `aws_resilience_hub_v2_service` registers a real deployable unit, its resources discovered from a CloudFormation stack, Terraform state, or an EKS cluster, under the next-generation AWS Resilience Hub model (launched May 2026), the counterpart to the original model's `aws_resilience_hub_app`, assessed against an `aws_resilience_hub_v2_policy`.
aws_resource_explorer2_default_view_asso: `aws_resource_explorer2_default_view_association` sets a real `aws_resource_explorer2_view` as the default for its AWS Region, so a search that doesn't explicitly name a view uses this one automatically.
aws_resource_explorer2_index: `aws_resource_explorer2_index` creates a real, per-Region search index for AWS Resource Explorer, the prerequisite that must exist in a Region before an `aws_resource_explorer2_view` can be created there.
aws_resource_explorer2_view: `aws_resource_explorer2_view` defines a real, filtered search scope over an `aws_resource_explorer2_index`, the resource that AWS Resource Explorer's own search queries are actually run against.
aws_resource_groups_group: `aws_resource_groups_group` creates a real named collection of AWS resources, defined by a tag-based or CloudFormation-stack-based query, so they can be viewed, tagged, and acted on together instead of individually.
aws_robo_maker_fleet: `aws_robo_maker_fleet` created a real logical grouping of physical robots that `aws_robo_maker_robot_application`s were deployed to together in AWS RoboMaker. AWS RoboMaker is now fully discontinued: AWS ended support on September 10, 2025, a date nearly a year in the past, steering customers toward AWS Batch for containerized simulation workloads instead; the project's own GitHub organization was archived in July 2026. This resource describes a service no longer operable rather than a current one.
aws_robo_maker_robot: `aws_robo_maker_robot` registered a real physical robot as a member of an `aws_robo_maker_fleet`. Like the rest of AWS RoboMaker, this describes a service AWS fully discontinued on September 10, 2025.
aws_robo_maker_robot_application: `aws_robo_maker_robot_application` defined a real robotics application, its code and dependent packages, that AWS RoboMaker deployed onto a fleet's robots or ran in simulation. AWS RoboMaker is now fully discontinued, having ended support on September 10, 2025.
aws_robo_maker_robot_application_version: `aws_robo_maker_robot_application_version` published a real, immutable version of an `aws_robo_maker_robot_application`. This describes the now fully discontinued AWS RoboMaker service, which ended support September 10, 2025.
aws_robo_maker_simulation_application: `aws_robo_maker_simulation_application` defined a real simulation environment, its code and rendering engine bundle, that AWS RoboMaker ran robotics applications against virtually before deploying to physical hardware. This describes the now fully discontinued AWS RoboMaker service, which ended support September 10, 2025.
aws_robo_maker_simulation_application_ve: `aws_robo_maker_simulation_application_version` published a real, immutable version of an `aws_robo_maker_simulation_application`. This describes the now fully discontinued AWS RoboMaker service, which ended support September 10, 2025.
aws_roles_anywhere_crl: `aws_roles_anywhere_crl` imports a real certificate revocation list into an `aws_roles_anywhere_trust_anchor`, so IAM Roles Anywhere rejects authentication attempts from any certificate that its issuing CA has since revoked.
aws_roles_anywhere_profile: `aws_roles_anywhere_profile` defines a real set of IAM roles and session policies that an `aws_roles_anywhere_trust_anchor`'s authenticated certificates are allowed to assume, the resource that actually maps a validated on-premises identity to AWS permissions.
aws_roles_anywhere_trust_anchor: `aws_roles_anywhere_trust_anchor` establishes real trust in a certificate authority, an AWS Private CA or an external CA, so that on-premises servers holding a certificate issued by it can authenticate to AWS and assume an `aws_roles_anywhere_profile`'s IAM role without long-lived access keys.
aws_route53_cidr_collection: `aws_route53_cidr_collection` defines a real, named collection of CIDR blocks that an `aws_route53_resolver_resolver_rule` or routing policy can reference by name, instead of listing raw IP ranges inline.
aws_route53_global_resolver_access_token: `aws_route53_global_resolver_access_token` issues a real credential that an authorized client uses to query an `aws_route53_global_resolver_global_resolver` from outside AWS, on-premises or over the internet, without a VPN or regional forwarding infrastructure.
aws_route53_global_resolver_dns_view: `aws_route53_global_resolver_dns_view` defines a real DNS view, which of an account's private hosted zones and rules apply, that an `aws_route53_global_resolver_global_resolver` resolves queries against for a given set of clients.
aws_route53_global_resolver_firewall_dom: `aws_route53_global_resolver_firewall_domain_list` defines a real list of domains that an `aws_route53_global_resolver_firewall_rule` matches DNS queries against on an `aws_route53_global_resolver_global_resolver`, the Global Resolver counterpart to `aws_route53_resolver_firewall_domain_list`.
aws_route53_global_resolver_firewall_rul: `aws_route53_global_resolver_firewall_rule` defines a real action, block, allow, alert, to take when a DNS query through an `aws_route53_global_resolver_global_resolver` matches an `aws_route53_global_resolver_firewall_domain_list`.
aws_route53_global_resolver_global_resol: `aws_route53_global_resolver_global_resolver` creates a real, internet-reachable anycast DNS resolver that resolves both public internet domains and an account's own Route 53 private hosted zones for authorized clients anywhere, on-premises data centers, branch offices, remote workers, without a VPN or per-Region forwarding setup. Route 53 Global Resolver reached general availability on March 9, 2026, roughly five months ago, so behavior here is verified live rather than assumed from general knowledge; resources must be managed in the US East (Ohio) Region regardless of where clients actually query from.
aws_route53_global_resolver_hosted_zone_: `aws_route53_global_resolver_hosted_zone_association` associates a real Route 53 private hosted zone with an `aws_route53_global_resolver_global_resolver`, so its records become resolvable through Global Resolver's own anycast endpoints for authorized external clients.
aws_route53_health_check: `aws_route53_health_check` creates a real, recurring health check against an endpoint, an IP address, domain, or CloudWatch alarm, that DNS failover routing and `aws_route53_record_set` health-check associations rely on to detect an unhealthy target.
aws_route53_hosted_zone: `aws_route53_hosted_zone` creates a real container for DNS records for a domain, public (resolvable on the internet) or private (resolvable only inside associated VPCs), that `aws_route53_record_set`s are created within.
aws_route53_profiles_profile: `aws_route53_profiles_profile` creates a real Route 53 Profile, a reusable bundle of DNS configuration, private hosted zone associations, Resolver rules, DNS Firewall rules, that can be applied consistently across many VPCs at once rather than configured VPC by VPC.
aws_route53_profiles_profile_association: `aws_route53_profiles_profile_association` attaches a real `aws_route53_profiles_profile` to a specific VPC, the resource that actually applies the profile's bundled DNS configuration to that VPC.
aws_route53_record_set: `aws_route53_record_set` creates a real DNS record, A, CNAME, MX, and more, including alias records that point at other AWS resources, within an `aws_route53_hosted_zone`.
aws_route53_record_set_group: `aws_route53_record_set_group` creates a real batch of `aws_route53_record_set`-equivalent DNS records within an `aws_route53_hosted_zone` in a single resource, useful when a template needs to manage many records together.
aws_route53_recovery_control_cluster: `aws_route53_recovery_control_cluster` creates a real, highly available cluster of Route 53 Application Recovery Controller endpoints across five AWS Regions, the redundant control plane that `aws_route53_recovery_control_control_panel`s and their routing controls depend on staying reachable during a regional outage.
aws_route53_recovery_control_control_pan: `aws_route53_recovery_control_control_panel` groups real routing controls under an `aws_route53_recovery_control_cluster`, the container that `aws_route53_recovery_control_safety_rule`s are evaluated against when a routing control is toggled during failover.
aws_route53_recovery_control_safety_rule: `aws_route53_recovery_control_safety_rule` defines a real constraint, such as requiring at least one routing control in a group to stay on, that an `aws_route53_recovery_control_control_panel` enforces to prevent an operator from accidentally toggling every control off at once during failover.
aws_route53_recovery_readiness_cell: `aws_route53_recovery_readiness_cell` groups real, Region-scoped `aws_route53_recovery_readiness_resource_set`s into a recoverable unit under Route 53 Application Recovery Controller's readiness-checking side, distinct from the routing-control side's `aws_route53_recovery_control_cluster`.
aws_route53_recovery_readiness_readiness: `aws_route53_recovery_readiness_readiness_check` continuously evaluates a real `aws_route53_recovery_readiness_resource_set` against a chosen readiness rule, capacity, configuration drift, and reports whether that set of resources is actually ready to take over if failover happened right now.
aws_route53_recovery_readiness_recovery_: `aws_route53_recovery_readiness_recovery_group` groups real `aws_route53_recovery_readiness_cell`s together, the top-level unit that Route 53 Application Recovery Controller reports overall multi-Region readiness for.
aws_route53_recovery_readiness_resource_: `aws_route53_recovery_readiness_resource_set` defines a real, named set of resources, load balancers, DynamoDB tables, and similar, in one Region that an `aws_route53_recovery_readiness_readiness_check` evaluates for failover readiness.
aws_route53_resolver_firewall_domain_lis: `aws_route53_resolver_firewall_domain_list` defines a real list of domains that an `aws_route53_resolver_firewall_rule_group`'s rules match outbound DNS queries against, inside a VPC, distinct from the newer Global Resolver's own `aws_route53_global_resolver_firewall_domain_list`.
aws_route53_resolver_firewall_rule_group: `aws_route53_resolver_firewall_rule_group` groups real DNS firewall rules, each matching an `aws_route53_resolver_firewall_domain_list` with an allow, block, or alert action, that an `aws_route53_resolver_firewall_rule_group_association` applies to a VPC's outbound DNS traffic.

`aws_route53_resolver_firewall_rule_group_association` applies a real `aws_route53_resolver_firewall_rule_group` to a specific VPC, the resource that actually turns the rule group's DNS filtering on for that VPC's traffic.
aws_route53_resolver_outpost_resolver: `aws_route53_resolver_outpost_resolver` creates a real DNS resolver running on an AWS Outposts rack, extending Route 53 Resolver's own hybrid DNS resolution to workloads on that on-premises Outpost.
aws_route53_resolver_resolver_endpoint: `aws_route53_resolver_resolver_endpoint` creates a real inbound or outbound DNS resolver endpoint in a VPC, the resource that lets on-premises DNS resolvers forward queries into that VPC, or lets the VPC forward queries out to on-premises DNS servers.
aws_route53_resolver_resolver_query_logg: `aws_route53_resolver_resolver_query_logging_config` configures real logging of DNS queries resolved through an `aws_route53_resolver_resolver_endpoint` or a VPC's default resolver, to a CloudWatch Logs group, S3 bucket, or Kinesis Data Firehose.
aws_route53_resolver_resolver_rule: `aws_route53_resolver_resolver_rule` defines a real forwarding rule that sends DNS queries for a specific domain out through an `aws_route53_resolver_resolver_endpoint` to a specified on-premises or other DNS server, rather than resolving them through Route 53's own default resolution.
aws_route53_resolver_resolver_rule_assoc: `aws_route53_resolver_resolver_rule_association` associates a real `aws_route53_resolver_resolver_rule` with a specific VPC, the resource that actually turns the rule's forwarding behavior on for that VPC's DNS queries.
aws_route_table: `aws_route_table` creates a real VPC route table, the set of routes that determines where network traffic from an associated subnet is directed.
aws_rtbfabric_inbound_external_link: `aws_rtbfabric_inbound_external_link` connects a real external bidder or exchange into an `aws_rtbfabric_responder_gateway`, the inbound counterpart within AWS RTB Fabric, manageable only through the RTB Fabric API, CLI, or CloudFormation rather than the console.
aws_rtbfabric_link: `aws_rtbfabric_link` creates a real, AWS-managed bidirectional connection component within AWS RTB Fabric, linking an `aws_rtbfabric_requester_gateway` to an `aws_rtbfabric_responder_gateway` for real-time bidding (RTB) advertising-exchange traffic. AWS RTB Fabric reached general availability in October 2025, roughly ten months ago, so behavior here is verified live rather than assumed from general knowledge.
aws_rtbfabric_link_routing_rule: `aws_rtbfabric_link_routing_rule` defines a real routing rule on an `aws_rtbfabric_link`, controlling how real-time bidding traffic flowing across that link is directed.
aws_rtbfabric_outbound_external_link: `aws_rtbfabric_outbound_external_link` connects a real `aws_rtbfabric_requester_gateway` out to an external bidder or exchange, the outbound counterpart to `aws_rtbfabric_inbound_external_link` within AWS RTB Fabric.
aws_rtbfabric_requester_gateway: `aws_rtbfabric_requester_gateway` creates a real gateway within AWS RTB Fabric that originates real-time bidding requests, the side of the fabric an ad exchange's own bid-request traffic enters through.
aws_rtbfabric_responder_gateway: `aws_rtbfabric_responder_gateway` creates a real gateway within AWS RTB Fabric that receives real-time bidding requests and returns bid responses, the side of the fabric a bidder's own infrastructure sits behind.
aws_rum_app_monitor: `aws_rum_app_monitor` creates a real CloudWatch RUM app monitor, a JavaScript snippet embedded in a web application that collects real client-side performance and error data, page load time, JS errors, HTTP request latency, from actual users' browsers.
aws_s3_access_grant: `aws_s3_access_grant` grants a real IAM principal or an IAM Identity Center user or group temporary, credential-vended access to a specific S3 prefix through an `aws_s3_access_grants_instance`, without writing or maintaining a bucket policy for that grant.
aws_s3_access_grants_instance: `aws_s3_access_grants_instance` creates a real, account-level S3 Access Grants instance, the resource that an `aws_s3_access_grants_location` and individual `aws_s3_access_grant`s are registered under to vend temporary, prefix-scoped S3 credentials.
aws_s3_access_grants_location: `aws_s3_access_grants_location` registers a real S3 bucket or prefix with an `aws_s3_access_grants_instance`, the scope that individual `aws_s3_access_grant`s are then issued against.
aws_s3_access_point: `aws_s3_access_point` creates a real, named network endpoint with its own access policy for an `aws_s3_bucket`, letting different applications reach the same bucket through different access points instead of managing one increasingly complex bucket policy.
aws_s3_bucket:
`aws_s3_bucket` creates the bucket itself. Versioning, encryption,
public-access blocking, and lifecycle rules are each their own separate
resource, attached to this bucket by reference, real Terraform provider
behavior since v4.
aws_s3_express_access_point: `aws_s3_express_access_point` creates a real access point scoped to an `aws_s3_express_directory_bucket`, S3 Express One Zone's own access-point resource.
aws_s3_express_directory_bucket: `aws_s3_express_directory_bucket` creates a real S3 Express One Zone bucket, storing data in a single Availability Zone with a directory-bucket structure for consistent, single-digit-millisecond request latency, distinct from a standard, multi-AZ `aws_s3_bucket`.
aws_s3_files_access_point: `aws_s3_files_access_point` creates a real access point scoped to an `aws_s3_files_file_system`, S3 Files' own access-point resource.
aws_s3_files_file_system: `aws_s3_files_file_system` creates a real, POSIX-compliant file system scoped to an S3 bucket or prefix, built on Amazon EFS technology, so that bucket's data can be mounted and accessed with full file-system semantics from EC2, ECS, EKS, or Lambda without the data ever leaving S3. Amazon S3 Files reached general availability on April 7, 2026, roughly four months ago, so behavior here is verified live rather than assumed from general knowledge.
aws_s3_files_file_system_policy: `aws_s3_files_file_system_policy` attaches a real resource-based access policy to an `aws_s3_files_file_system`, controlling which principals can mount and access it as a file system.
aws_s3_multi_region_access_point: `aws_s3_multi_region_access_point` creates a real, single global endpoint that routes requests to the closest of several `aws_s3_bucket`s replicated across multiple Regions, so an application can use one endpoint regardless of which Region actually serves a given request.
aws_s3_object_lambda_access_point: `aws_s3_object_lambda_access_point` creates a real access point in front of an existing `aws_s3_access_point` that runs a Lambda function against each GET response before it reaches the caller, letting data be transformed, redacted, or enriched on the fly without a separate copy of the object.
aws_s3_outposts_access_point: `aws_s3_outposts_access_point` creates a real access point scoped to an `aws_s3_outposts_bucket`, controlling which VPC and principals can reach that Outposts bucket.
aws_s3_outposts_bucket: `aws_s3_outposts_bucket` creates a real S3 bucket physically located on an AWS Outposts rack, for workloads that must keep S3-compatible storage on premises rather than in an AWS Region.
aws_s3_outposts_endpoint: `aws_s3_outposts_endpoint` creates a real network endpoint on an AWS Outposts rack's local network that lets on-premises applications reach an `aws_s3_outposts_bucket` without traffic leaving the Outpost.
aws_s3_storage_lens: `aws_s3_storage_lens` creates a real S3 Storage Lens configuration, an organization- or account-wide dashboard of storage usage and activity metrics across every `aws_s3_bucket` in scope, including cost-optimization recommendations.
aws_s3_storage_lens_group: `aws_s3_storage_lens_group` defines a real, filtered subset of objects, by prefix, tag, size, or age, within an `aws_s3_storage_lens` configuration, so its metrics can be broken out for just that subset instead of only whole-bucket totals.
aws_s3_tables_table: `aws_s3_tables_table` creates a real Apache Iceberg table within an `aws_s3_tables_table_bucket`, with S3 Tables handling the table's own compaction, snapshot management, and file optimization automatically in the background.
aws_s3_tables_table_bucket: `aws_s3_tables_table_bucket` creates a real S3 Tables bucket, a bucket type purpose-built to store Apache Iceberg tables rather than arbitrary objects, that `aws_s3_tables_table`s are created inside.
aws_s3_vectors_index: `aws_s3_vectors_index` creates a real vector index within an S3 vector bucket, storing and querying up to two billion embeddings per index natively in S3 for similarity search, commonly used as the storage layer behind a Bedrock knowledge base rather than a separate vector database. Amazon S3 Vectors reached general availability in December 2025, roughly eight months ago, so behavior here is verified live rather than assumed from general knowledge.
aws_sage_maker_action: `aws_sage_maker_action` records a real, tracked action, a training job run or model deployment, in SageMaker's ML Lineage Tracking graph, connecting the artifacts, datasets, and models it consumed and produced so a model's full provenance can be traced later.
aws_sage_maker_algorithm: `aws_sage_maker_algorithm` registers a real, reusable training algorithm, packaged as a Docker image with defined input channels and hyperparameters, that can be published to AWS Marketplace or reused across SageMaker training jobs without re-specifying the underlying container each time.
aws_sqs_queue:
Amazon SQS is a fully managed message queue. `aws_sqs_queue` creates
and configures one, standard or FIFO, with a real, typed binding in
every SDK language.
aws_vpc:
`aws_vpc` creates a real, isolated virtual network, the real
foundation every other real networked resource, subnets, security
groups, route tables, gets placed inside.
